body: Most coverage is from a Generation 3 trekker, which is lower to the ground and often on sidewalks. Some indoor tripod coverage also exists.
Spanish is the official language. Uniquely, Costa Rica is the only trekker-only country where Spanish is the main language.
Costa Rican licence plates are short, white, and have blue text, which may appear as a light blue tint when blurred.
Utility poles are typically round and made of concrete.
Stop signs use the word "ALTO", similar to Mexico and Guatemala.
Coverage is very limited, mostly around San José and the northern west coast. There's also coverage on Cocos Island and a boat trekker near Caño Island.
Beach trekkers are mostly on the northern east coast, but also west of San José and on Cocos Island.
Rural forest trekkers are mostly in central Costa Rica. Cocos Island is also covered in dense tropical forests.
Urban coverage is mainly in San José and Cartago, with some in Liberia and Filadelfia de Guanacaste.
The Children's Museum in northern San José has a grand castle-like exterior.
Near the National Museum are wealthy-looking homes and a tower resembling a medieval European fortress.
An orange pedestrian bridge crosses a highway at Parque de la Paz in southeastern San José.
La Sabana Park contains several sports facilities, including the National Stadium in the west.
The University of Costa Rica in eastern San José is a busy campus with lots of greenery and medium-sized buildings.
Palacio de los Deportes in Heredia is a stadium with a boxy look and a red, blue, and white color scheme.
At the Juan Santamaría International Airport, the trekker is on a four-lane road and outside the terminal.
In Centro Recreativo Bosque de la Hoja, the trekker is followed by three dogs through a pine forest.
Recreational Park Los Manantiales has roads lined with sugarcane plantations and cornstalk dracaena plants.
Laguna de Fraijanes Recreational Park has a large orange wooden gate at its entrance and is situated around a small lagoon.
The Cartago Municipal Museum has a palace-like facade, a garden, and a railway in the street out front.
The Ruins of Cartago are the remains of a large Catholic church near the city center.
The José Rafael "Fello" Meza Ivankovich Stadium in southern Cartago is recognizable by its surrounding dark blue walls.
The Costa Rica Institute of Technology is often recognizable by the mountain range visible to the south and east.
The entrance to Jardín Botanico Lankester has a dirt road and a sign. Inside, the garden has many different plants and curvy walkways.
The Punta Leona Resort has a distinctive red brick pavement with bricks shaped like those commonly found in Turkey.
Coverage in Liberia is recognizable by a white building with rounded windows and brown wooden frames, visible in all local coverage.
In Filadelfia de Guanacaste, coverage is often on the edge of a park with a red brick pavement where bricks are in an "L" shape.
